prompt: A design note for a clinic appointment-scheduling module replaces the existing relational tables with an event-sourced store, justified only as 'this will scale to hospital-network load and makes audit trivial'. No target load is quantified anywhere, no quality-attribute scenario or response measure exists, and the change is queued to merge on that claim alone.
location_hint: Design note justifying the persistence choice for the scheduling module
rationale: Verbatim SD-Q-1 signal: quality claims ('will scale', 'audit trivial') justify a design decision yet carry no proof, scenario, or response measure — the 'block unsupported design' variant, since the merge rests on the unproven claim.

prompt: A log-parsing library's module header pledges the NFR 'parses multi-gigabyte input within a 512 MB memory ceiling', and maintainers cite that pledge when rejecting a simpler implementation. Nothing in the test suite, CI, or any benchmark measures peak memory, so the ceiling has never been validated.
location_hint: Parser module header NFR plus the absent memory benchmark in tests/CI
rationale: A stated NFR lacks any measured scenario or response measure, and it actively steers design decisions — exactly the SD-Q-1 signal of an NFR without proof.

prompt: A file-sync engine merges a rewritten conflict-resolution path with a changelog entry claiming 'zero data loss and no user-visible latency impact'. There is no test demonstrating the no-data-loss property, no before/after latency measurement, and the design page's tradeoff section is marked TBD.
location_hint: Changelog claim and the conflict-resolution module's design page
rationale: Two quality claims (reliability and latency) ship with no proof and an explicitly unstated tradeoff — the smallest action (state force, tradeoff, and validation, or write a measured scenario) applies directly.

prompt: A shipping-rate service fixes a duplicate-zone bug by re-keying the rate table on zone id, replacing a linear scan with a keyed lookup as a side effect. The commit, comments, and docs describe only the correctness fix, assert no performance, scalability, or reliability property, and no NFR is stated for this path.
location_hint: Rate-table lookup change in the shipping-rate calculator
rationale: Grounded in the guard's first half: 'no quality claim'. The lookup swap looks like an optimization someone might demand benchmarks for, but no quality claim or NFR exists, so SD-Q-1 has nothing that requires proof.

prompt: A telemetry-ingestion gateway documents the NFR 'sustain 5,000 events/s with p99 end-to-end latency under 200 ms'. A nightly CI load test replays a recorded 5,000 events/s stream against a staging deployment, asserts the p99 response measure, and archives results per build.
location_hint: Gateway NFR doc and the nightly load-test scenario
rationale: Grounded in the guard's second half: 'an NFR that already has a measured scenario'. The bold throughput/latency claim baits the smell, but a repeatable scenario with an asserted response measure already backs it.

prompt: A product-catalog service has carried a read-through in-process cache decorator on category lookups for eight months. It emits no hit-rate, staleness, or latency metric, nobody is named as its owner, and the only way to turn it off is editing code and redeploying — nobody can say whether it still helps or how stale data is bounded.
location_hint: Caching decorator on the catalog category-lookup read path
rationale: A quality tactic (cache) with no measurement, no owner, and no rollback — the verbatim SD-Q-2 signal; the smallest action (add metric, owner, and rollback or remove the tactic) applies exactly.

prompt: A payroll-export job groups ledger writes into hard-coded batches of 500, introduced for database-load reasons by a developer who has since left. No metric captures batch latency or database load before or after, no flag or config path restores row-at-a-time writes, and no owner is recorded for the tuning.
location_hint: Batch-write loop and its hard-coded constant in the payroll-export job
rationale: Batching is a performance tactic that lacks measurement, owner, and rollback, so nobody can validate it still earns its complexity or safely revert it — SD-Q-2.

prompt: A media-transcoding orchestrator wraps its metadata-service calls in a hand-rolled circuit breaker with hard-coded thresholds (open after 5 failures, half-open after 30 s). Breaker state and trip frequency are exported nowhere, no one owns the thresholds, and a misfiring breaker can only be corrected by editing constants and redeploying.
location_hint: Circuit-breaker wrapper around metadata-service calls in the orchestrator
rationale: An availability tactic at a single layer (so not stacked handling) with no measurement, owner, or rollback — SD-Q-2's unmeasured-tactic signal.

prompt: A document-search service fronts index queries with a read-through cache that exports hit-rate and staleness metrics to a dashboard reviewed by the search-infra team, which the service catalog lists as the cache's owner. A per-environment config flag disables the cache, and that rollback runbook was exercised last quarter.
location_hint: Read-through cache on the document-index query path
rationale: Grounded in the guard: 'measured tactic with owner and rollback'. A cache invites the reflex flag, but measurement, a named owner, and an exercised rollback are all present, so the tactic is governed.

prompt: An IoT-ingestion pipeline partitions device streams across eight shards. Per-shard lag and skew are exported with alerts, the platform team is the named owner in the service catalog, capacity results from the last game-day are archived, and a documented repartitioning runbook plus a single-shard degraded mode provide the way back.
location_hint: Stream-partitioning layer of the IoT-ingestion pipeline
rationale: Grounded in the guard: the sharding tactic is measured (lag/skew metrics, archived capacity runs), owned, and has a rehearsed rollback path, so 'measured tactic with owner and rollback' clears it.

prompt: A customer-data platform must erase personal records within 30 days of a deletion request. The API team assumes the nightly cleanup job satisfies it, the cleanup job covers only the primary store, and nothing owns erasure in the analytics replica or the export bucket — no boundary or team is named as owning the end-to-end requirement.
location_hint: Erasure requirement versus the api service, cleanup job, analytics replica, and export bucket
rationale: A quality requirement floats with no owning boundary; each part assumes another covers it, leaving stores uncovered — the verbatim SD-Q-3 signal, fixed by assigning or splitting the NFR across owners.

prompt: A ticket-booking flow carries a stated end-to-end checkout budget of 800 ms across the web gateway, seat-inventory service, and payment adapter, but no per-service allocation exists and no boundary owns the budget. A PR adding a third downstream call is being argued over against 'the 800 ms rule' that no service owns.
location_hint: End-to-end latency budget spanning gateway, seat-inventory, and payment boundaries
rationale: An NFR that gates the change under review has no owning boundary or allocation — SD-Q-3's block variant ('an NFR that gates the change but has no owner').

prompt: A warehouse system's compliance doc requires every stock mutation to appear in the audit trail. The design review shows engineers disagreeing over whether the stock module, the event-bus consumer, or individual callers own that guarantee; no boundary is assigned, and today the requirement holds only on paths that happen to emit events.
location_hint: Audit-completeness requirement versus the stock module / event-consumer ownership decision
rationale: The quality requirement (audit completeness) has contested, unassigned ownership, so satisfaction is accidental — the human+static evidence pattern of an unallocated NFR.

prompt: A fleet-routing platform states a 99.9% availability NFR for route computation. The service catalog names the routing-engine boundary as its owner, the routing team runs the error-budget dashboard, and dependent services consume routing through its API with their own documented degraded modes.
location_hint: Availability NFR entry for the routing-engine boundary
rationale: Grounded in the guard's first half: 'owning boundary named'. The NFR reads like a lofty doc-level target, but it is allocated to the routing engine with visible ownership artifacts, so nothing is unallocated.

prompt: A PR adds a read-only reporting endpoint to a benefits-enrollment service. The org-wide disaster-recovery requirement (15-minute RPO) appears in the platform handbook and no module in this repo claims it, but DR is owned and tracked at the platform layer outside this codebase, and the stateless endpoint does not alter recovery characteristics.
location_hint: New read-only reporting endpoint in the benefits-enrollment service
rationale: Grounded in the guard: 'owning boundary named, or requirement out of current scope'. The RPO requirement is out of scope for this change and owned at the platform layer, so blocking the endpoint over it would be a false positive.

prompt: In an order-placement chain, the HTTP wrapper retries payment-gateway calls 3 times with backoff, the checkout service retries the whole operation 3 more times on timeout, and the job queue redelivers failed checkout jobs up to 5 times. No layer is documented as owning retries, no overall attempt budget exists, and payment capture carries no idempotency key, so one slow gateway response can multiply into dozens of capture attempts.
location_hint: Retry configuration across the HTTP wrapper, checkout service, and job-queue redelivery
rationale: Retries repeat across three layers of one call chain with no owning layer or budget over a non-idempotent operation — the block variant of SD-Q-4 ('stacked retries on non-idempotent operations').

prompt: A weather-dashboard read path lets the widget fall back to cached data after 2 s, while the aggregation service wraps the upstream call in its own 10 s timeout with a stale-data fallback, and the upstream client library retries twice with 8 s timeouts. Inner budgets exceed the outer one, so the widget's fallback always fires while inner layers keep working invisibly, and no layer owns the policy or an end-to-end budget.
location_hint: Timeout and fallback settings in the widget, aggregation service, and upstream client
rationale: Timeouts and fallbacks repeat across layers of one call chain with no owning layer and mutually incoherent budgets — the verbatim SD-Q-4 signal (warn flavor on a read path).

prompt: A nightly inventory sync stacks three retry layers: the vendor-feed client retries 4 times internally, the sync service wraps each item update in a 3-attempt loop, and the scheduler re-runs the whole job on nonzero exit. Updates apply stock deltas rather than absolute quantities, and no document names an owning layer or a total attempt budget, so partial failures can apply the same delta repeatedly.
location_hint: Vendor-feed client retries, per-item retry loop in the sync service, and the scheduler re-run policy
rationale: Stacked retries across a batch call chain with no owner or budget over non-idempotent delta updates — multiplied attempts corrupt stock counts, the SD-Q-4 block variant.

prompt: A notification-dispatch chain documents the outbox worker as the single owner of failure handling with an explicit budget: 5 attempts within 30 s, then dead-letter. Every send carries an idempotency key the provider adapter deduplicates on (covered by tests), attempt and dead-letter rates are graphed, and the HTTP client and queue are explicitly configured to 0 retries with comments linking the ownership doc.
location_hint: Retry-capable settings visible in the outbox worker, HTTP client, and queue configuration
rationale: Grounded in the guard: 'one documented owning layer with an explicit budget and idempotence evidence'. Retry-capable knobs appear at three layers, baiting a stacking call, but only one layer actually retries and every guard element is present.

prompt: A report-generation service is the documented owner of retrying render-engine calls: 2 attempts inside a 10 s budget. Renders are idempotent by content hash with dedupe verified in tests, while the HTTP client sets only connect/read timeouts with zero retries and the queue delivers at-most-once.
location_hint: Service-layer retry policy plus bare transport timeouts in the render-engine client
rationale: Grounded in the guard: a bare transport timeout beneath the documented owning layer is not a second failure-handling layer; ownership, an explicit budget, and idempotence evidence all exist, so nothing is stacked.

prompt: A storefront checkout improvement states its NFR as a measured scenario — p95 checkout under 600 ms at 200 rps, asserted by the CI load test — and allocates per-hop budgets with the checkout service named as the owning boundary. Its new response cache ships with hit-rate and staleness metrics, a named owner, and a kill-switch flag, and failure handling lives in the gateway alone under a documented 3-attempt/2 s budget over idempotency-keyed calls, with retries disabled elsewhere.
location_hint: Checkout design doc, cache decorator, and gateway failure-handling policy
rationale: Every group concern is satisfied: the quality claim has a measured scenario with a response measure (Q-1 guard), the cache tactic is measured, owned, and rollbackable (Q-2 guard), the NFR is allocated to a named boundary with per-hop budgets (Q-3 guard), and failure handling has one documented owning layer with budget and idempotence evidence (Q-4 guard).

prompt: A currency-conversion library documents its only NFR — half-even rounding to 4 decimal places — with a property-based test sweeping a million random amount/rate pairs in CI, and its README names the library itself as the sole owner of rounding correctness. The conversion path is pure computation with no caches, retries, timeouts, or fallbacks.
location_hint: Library README NFR statement and the property-based rounding test
rationale: The stated quality requirement has a measured scenario and a named owning boundary, and no quality tactic or failure-handling layer exists to be unmeasured or stacked — nothing in SD-Q-1 through SD-Q-4 applies.

prompt: A billing system computes VAT exemption with the same inline conditional — customer kind is NONPROFIT and region group is EU, plus a hardcoded revenue threshold — repeated in invoice_builder.py, quote_estimator.py, refund_calculator.py, and reports/csv_export.py. History shows the last exemption-policy change was one commit editing all four files, and a fifth copy in dunning/notice_text.py was missed and still applies the old threshold.
location_hint: repeated VAT-exemption conditional in invoice_builder.py, quote_estimator.py, refund_calculator.py, reports/csv_export.py, and the stale copy in dunning/notice_text.py
rationale: One exemption rule has five hand-copied decision sites and no owning module; history shows a policy change fanning out into a multi-file edit that still missed a site — the shotgun-change signal on both history and static layers, with no migration-with-exit story to excuse the scatter.

prompt: A field-service scheduler embeds its bookable-window rule (Mon–Fri, tenant holiday list, last slot 16:30) as separately copy-pasted checks in slot search, reminder emailing, SLA-clock start, and the partner availability formatter. Moving the cutoff from 17:00 to 16:30 last month took one commit touching all four modules, and review comments show the team keeps a manual checklist of 'places to update when hours change'.
location_hint: duplicated bookable-window checks in slot search, reminder emailing, SLA-clock start, and the partner availability formatter
rationale: A single scheduling rule fans every change into four coordinated edits, and the team compensates with a human checklist instead of a rule owner — one rule requiring scattered edits, evidenced by the multi-module commit; nothing marks this as a migration in progress.

prompt: A log-ingestion system enforces its maximum accepted record size and permitted encoding set as literal constants restated in the TCP receiver, the file-batch importer, the replay tool, and two test helpers — six sites by grep. A proposal to raise the limit from 1 MiB to 4 MiB has stalled because nobody can confidently enumerate every enforcement point.
location_hint: the six restated record-size/encoding literals across the TCP receiver, batch importer, replay tool, and test helpers
rationale: The acceptance rule has no owning definition, so one rule change requires six scattered edits and change is already stalling — SD-E-1's 'one rule requires scattered edits', with the multiplied-site count pushing toward its block severity.

prompt: A retail pricing rule used to be inlined at five call sites; a centralization effort extracted it into a PricingPolicy owner two sprints ago. Three legacy call sites still hold the inline copy, each annotated with the migration ticket; the plan names an owning team, converts sites incrementally (two already done), sets an end-of-quarter completion date, and a CI lint blocks any new inline copy.
location_hint: the three annotated legacy inline copies pending conversion to PricingPolicy
rationale: SD-E-1's guard is 'migration with exit': the remaining scatter is a shrinking, owned migration remnant with tracked tickets, a deadline, and a lint preventing regression — flagging it as shotgun change (or as a migration without exit) would be a false positive.

prompt: A device-sync service added a LegacyPayloadAdapter two years ago to translate v1 sync envelopes while clients moved to v2. Both paths are still fully maintained: every new field must be added to the v2 model and mirrored into the adapter's v1 mapping, the adapter carries its own test suite, and no ticket, metric, or client-version threshold defines when v1 handling can be deleted.
location_hint: LegacyPayloadAdapter and the parallel v1/v2 envelope handling in the sync service
rationale: A compatibility shim with no removal path: two years of dual maintenance where every change is paid twice, and no owner, trigger, or deadline exists for deleting the v1 path — SD-E-2's signal, trending into its 'permanent dual path' block condition.

prompt: A payroll service began migrating employee records from a wide staff table to a normalized schema; a DualWriteRepository writes both schemas and reads prefer the new one with fallback to the old. Eighteen months later the fallback read remains, every mutation still writes the old table, the engineer who started the migration has left, and no completion criterion — backfill verification, cutover date, or fallback-hit metric — is defined anywhere.
location_hint: DualWriteRepository's write-both/read-fallback paths spanning the legacy staff table and the normalized schema
rationale: The migration lost its exit: dual write plus fallback read persist with no owner, trigger, or deadline, so the compatibility path is on track to become permanent — the core SD-E-2 signal on static (two live paths) and history (18 months, departed owner) evidence.

prompt: An inventory service is mid-migration from XML to JSON stock feeds, with a translation shim converting the remaining XML suppliers. The shim landed six weeks ago; MIGRATION.md names the owning team, lists the four suppliers left (down from eleven), schedules shim removal for the first sprint after the last supplier confirms JSON, and a dashboard counts XML requests per day so the trigger is observable.
location_hint: the XML-to-JSON translation shim for the four remaining suppliers
rationale: SD-E-2's guard — a short migration with owner, trigger, and deadline — is met verbatim: the shim is young, shrinking, owned, and has an observable removal trigger with a scheduled collapse, so a removal path clearly exists.

prompt: An e-commerce checkout module reads nine boolean feature flags (new_address_form, retry_capture_v2, gift_wrap_beta, …). Five have been enabled at 100% in every environment for over a year, two guard branches whose disabled side no longer compiles against current models, and the flag registry records no owner, expiry, or cleanup ticket for any entry; flag-combination branching is now the main source of untested paths.
location_hint: the nine long-lived flag checks in the checkout module and the ownerless flag registry
rationale: Flags lack owner, expiry, and return path: fully-ramped flags still fork the code a year on and dead branches rot behind them — a textbook pile-up well past the 'short rollout with owner and trigger' guard, at the 'permanent flags' block edge.

prompt: A notification dispatcher has grown a toggles.yaml of fourteen entries mixing experiment flags, kill switches, and per-tenant workarounds (tenant_442_skip_quiet_hours, sms_provider_b_rollout, digest_rewrite_enabled). Nothing distinguishes temporary from permanent; the sms provider rollout finished last quarter yet both provider paths remain, tenant workarounds were added without tickets, and no entry records an owner or removal condition.
location_hint: toggles.yaml and its flag branches in the notification dispatcher, including the completed-but-uncollapsed sms rollout
rationale: An unclassified, unowned flag registry where completed rollouts never collapse and ad-hoc workarounds accrete is SD-E-3's exact signal; even legitimately permanent kill switches need an owner and classification, and none here has either.

prompt: A video-transcoding pipeline gates codec selection, GPU offload, and watermarking behind seven 'experiment' flags evaluated deep in the worker loop. The experiments concluded months ago (their analytics dashboards were deleted), but the flags now serve as the de facto production configuration, set via environment variables documented only in a runbook, with no owner and no plan to either promote them to real configuration or remove them.
location_hint: the seven concluded experiment flags inside the transcoding worker loop acting as permanent configuration
rationale: Concluded experiments with no return path: the flags outlived their trigger, lost their owner, and silently became permanent configuration — the 'flags lack owner, expiry, or return path' signal and SD-E-3's permanent-flag block condition.

prompt: A ride-booking service introduced a single flag, surge_calc_v2, three weeks ago for a staged rollout: the flag definition names the owning team and links the rollout ticket, ramp sits at 50% behind an error-rate guardrail, and the ticket's exit criterion deletes the flag and the v1 path after seven days at 100%. The previous two rollout flags from this playbook were removed on schedule.
location_hint: the surge_calc_v2 rollout flag and its temporary v1/v2 dual path
rationale: This is SD-E-3's guard verbatim — a short rollout with owner and trigger — plus demonstrated removal discipline; one in-flight, owned rollout flag (and its bounded dual path) must not be reported as pile-up or as a migration without exit.

prompt: A shared date library marks its FiscalCalendar class deprecated with the note 'do not use' and no pointer to a replacement; forty-one call sites across three services still use it because nothing else provides fiscal-week math. The annotation is two years old, its author has left, consumer builds suppress the warning wholesale, and no ticket tracks removal.
location_hint: the deprecated FiscalCalendar class in the shared date library and its 41 warning-suppressed call sites
rationale: A deprecated element lacking replacement, owner, and removal trigger, with live consumers who have normalized suppressing the warning — SD-E-4's block condition: permanent deprecation with live consumers and no plan.

prompt: A ticketing platform's plugin SDK declares its v3 hook interface deprecated in the changelog and README, yet new convenience helpers built on v3 keep shipping, the promised v4 interface exists only as a design document, and partners asking when v3 ends are told there is no date. Deprecation warnings log on every plugin load, but no consumer count, sunset trigger, or owning team is recorded.
location_hint: the deprecated-yet-still-growing v3 hook interface in the plugin SDK
rationale: The deprecation has no lifecycle — replacement unshipped, owner absent, removal trigger undefined — and history contradicts the announcement (the deprecated surface still accretes features), matching SD-E-4's signal on static and history layers.

prompt: A geo-utilities module deprecates distanceMiles() in favor of the already-shipped distance(unit): the deprecation note names the replacement and the owning team, a codemod migrated all in-repo callers, remaining external callers are tracked by a telemetry counter, and the documented trigger removes the function two releases after that counter reads zero for 30 days.
location_hint: the deprecated distanceMiles() shim awaiting its telemetry-triggered removal
rationale: SD-E-4's guard — staged deprecation with owner, replacement, and removal trigger — is satisfied on every element: replacement shipped and named, owner named, trigger observable with a scheduled removal; this is the healthy lifecycle, not the smell.

prompt: An inventory service runs a web framework major that left long-term support two years ago and is now four majors behind current; the lockfile has not been regenerated in 14 months and the package manager's 'outdated' report sits in a TODO from last year. No team, cadence, or policy owns dependency currency — upgrades happen only when a build breaks.
location_hint: the four-majors-behind framework pin and 14-month-old lockfile; no upgrade cadence or owner anywhere in the service
rationale: A dependency far behind its supported line with no cadence and no owner, decaying reactively — SD-E-5's first prong on history and human evidence; the finding is the missing currency practice itself (specific vulnerability exposure would delegate to devsecops-audit).

prompt: A payments team plans to move its ORM from major version 4 to major version 9 in one release, bundling the runtime bump and a schema-annotation rewrite into a single branch that is already three months old and touches roughly 600 files. Each intermediate major is installable and has a published migration guide, so stepping 4→5→…→9 behind the existing test suite is feasible, but was rejected as slower.
location_hint: the single long-lived 4→9 ORM upgrade branch in the payments service
rationale: A big-bang upgrade where incremental is demonstrably feasible (installable intermediates with migration guides) — SD-E-5's second prong; the smallest action is decomposing the jump into stepwise, testable upgrades.

prompt: A telemetry-ingestion service pins its message-broker client one minor version behind latest. A quarterly dependency review owned by the platform team is on the calendar and in CONTRIBUTING.md, a currency dashboard reports how far each dependency trails its line, and the one-minor lag is a recorded, dated decision waiting out a known regression in the newest client, with the upgrade ticket already scheduled.
location_hint: the deliberately pinned, one-minor-behind broker client under the owned quarterly review
rationale: SD-E-5's guard — measured currency with an upgrade cadence and owner — is met: a dashboard measures drift, a named owner runs a quarterly cadence, and the small lag is a deliberate, dated, ticketed decision, not unowned staleness.

prompt: A shipping-rate service keeps every rate rule in one RateBook module that all consumers call, with a lint forbidding inline copies; last quarter's carrier-feed migration ran to a dated plan and its shim was deleted at cutover (visible in history). The only active flag is a week-old owned rollout with a written exit criterion, past deprecations shipped a replacement and were removed once their telemetry trigger fired, and a named owner reviews dependency currency monthly against a dashboard.
rationale: Every evolution concern appears in its healthy form — single rule owner, migration collapsed at its exit, one short owned flag, full deprecation lifecycles, measured dependency cadence — so a review should raise none of SD-E-1 through SD-E-5.

prompt: A small internal CSV-deduplication utility (about 800 lines, two contributors) has no feature flags, no deprecated surface, and no compatibility shims; its dedup rules live in a single rules.py consulted by both the CLI and the library entry point. Its three dependencies are on current stable releases, refreshed alongside the platform's routine monthly image rebuild.
rationale: Absence of evolution machinery is not a smell: rules have one home, nothing is deprecated or shimmed, no flags exist, and dependencies are current under a routine refresh — none of the SD-E signals fire, and a reviewer must not demand ceremony where no debt exists.

prompt: Review the appointment package of a clinic-scheduling service: the same bookable time interval is modeled as `Slot` in availability.ts, renamed to `Window` in reservation.ts, and rendered as `openingBlock` in the notification templates, with field-by-field mapping functions between them that change only the names. All three files live in one package maintained by one team, and a comment in reservation.ts reads 'Window == Slot'.
location_hint: availability.ts `Slot` vs reservation.ts `Window` vs notification templates `openingBlock`, all in one package
rationale: One concept carries three synonymous names inside a single context — the rename-only mappers and the 'Window == Slot' comment prove there is no semantic difference and no bounded context, so the guard (bounded context plus translator) cannot apply; this is SD-S-1's 'conflicting term or synonym' signal, fixed by rename/qualify.

prompt: Review a warehouse service where `quantity` means units-on-hand in StockLevel records but units-per-case-pack in PackagingSpec records; ReplenishmentCalculator.plan() accepts both as bare `quantity: number` parameters, and last month a case-pack value was passed into the on-hand comparison, ordering 24x too much stock. The public /stock endpoint also returns a top-level `quantity` field without stating which meaning it carries.
location_hint: `quantity` in StockLevel vs PackagingSpec, the plan() parameters, and the /stock API response field
rationale: One term carries two conflicting meanings (a homonym rather than a synonym), the ambiguity already produced a wrong computation, and it leaks into an ambiguous public field — SD-S-1's contract-blur block variant; the smallest action is to qualify the names (onHandUnits vs unitsPerCasePack).

prompt: Review a CRM where the Sales bounded context models a person as `Prospect` and the Support bounded context models the same human as `Requester`; each context has its own package with its own documented glossary, and the only integration point is SupportIntake.fromProspect(), an anti-corruption translator invoked when a closed deal becomes a support account. Nothing else crosses the boundary.
location_hint: sales/Prospect vs support/Requester with SupportIntake.fromProspect() as the sole crossing
rationale: Two names for one human is SD-S-1's surface signal, but the false_positive_guard — 'bounded context plus translator' — is satisfied exactly: the terms live in separate documented bounded contexts and a single anti-corruption translator owns the only crossing, so no finding should be reported.

prompt: Review a billing service where quoting/discount.py and invoicing/discount.py each define a Discount class that began as a copy-paste two years ago: the quoting copy now caps percentage discounts at 100% and rounds half-up while the invoicing copy accepts any percentage and truncates, and quotes convert to invoices by copying discount fields straight across with no translation. Finance has reported invoices occasionally a cent below the agreed quote and one negative-total invoice.
location_hint: quoting/discount.py vs invoicing/discount.py and the quote-to-invoice field copy
rationale: The same concept diverged across two models inside one service after an accidental copy-paste, and the untranslated field copy carries values across incompatible invariants (cap and rounding) — SD-S-2's invariant-mismatch block variant; neither an intentional boundary nor a translator exists, so the guard fails.

prompt: Review a courier-dispatch service where order_intake's Address gained a validated ISO country code and normalized postcode last quarter while label_printing still uses its original free-text Address copy; a nightly sync copies intake addresses into label records field-by-field, so an order stored with country 'DE' prints the literal string 'DE' on the label, and unvalidated legacy label addresses flow back into intake on returns.
location_hint: order_intake.Address vs label_printing.Address and the nightly bidirectional field-copy sync
rationale: One concept (Address) drifted between two in-service models — one received normalization and validation the other never did — and the untranslated bidirectional copy leaks each model's assumptions into the other; SD-S-2's 'same concept diverges across models', requiring convergence or an explicit translation.

prompt: Review the integration between an Ordering microservice and a Fulfillment microservice that each define their own OrderLine model on purpose: Fulfillment's adds pickLocation and drops all pricing fields, an ADR records that the two contexts evolve independently, and the only crossing is FulfillmentTranslator.toPickLine(orderLine) in the integration layer, pinned by contract tests.
location_hint: ordering.OrderLine vs fulfillment.OrderLine with FulfillmentTranslator.toPickLine() at the boundary
rationale: Two diverging OrderLine models look like duplicate concept drift, but the guard — 'intentional boundary copy with translator' — is met: the per-context copy is a documented deliberate decision and a tested translator owns the only crossing, so the divergence is designed, not drift; nothing should be flagged.

prompt: Review a payments module that deserializes the payment provider's webhook JSON straight into its persisted Payment entity: provider field names (txn_ref, amt_minor) and provider status strings like 'AUTH_HOLD' and 'CAPT_PEND' are stored as-is and branched on across refund logic, reporting, and the ledger. A recent provider API revision renamed two fields and split one status, breaking refund-eligibility checks deep in the domain layer.
location_hint: webhook deserialization into the persisted Payment entity and the vendor-status branches in refund/ledger logic
rationale: The external provider's wire shape became internal state and vocabulary — domain logic branches on vendor status strings, and a vendor rename broke deep domain code — exactly SD-S-4's 'external shape becomes internal state'; this is domain-rule-bearing data, not a stable CRUD meaning, so the guard fails and edge translation is owed.

prompt: Review a fleet-tracking service whose canonical VehiclePosition table mirrors the GPS vendor's record layout verbatim, including vendor quality-flag codes and the vendor convention that latitude/longitude may be null when fix quality is 'Q0'; trip-scoring and geofence rules read the vendor flags directly and assume coordinates are always present, which caused null-coordinate crashes when a new device model started emitting Q0 rows.
location_hint: VehiclePosition persistence mirroring the vendor record; vendor-flag branches in trip scoring and geofencing
rationale: An external device-vendor shape is stored as canonical internal state and its looser invariants (nullable coordinates) contradict what domain rules assume — SD-S-4's invariant-mismatch block variant; translating at the edge into a model whose invariants the domain owns is the smallest action.

prompt: Review an internal help-center admin app that manages FAQ entries through a headless content store: the store's FaqEntry shape {id, question, answer, updatedAt} is used directly as the app's model across the list, edit, and save screens. No business rule branches on the content, the shape has been unchanged for four years, and the app's only job is create/read/update/delete of these display records.
location_hint: FaqEntry used directly across the admin app's CRUD screens
rationale: An external store shape used as the internal model is SD-S-4's surface signal, but the guard — 'stable CRUD meaning' — applies: the record is long-stable display content with pure CRUD semantics and no domain invariants, so an edge-translation layer would add cost without protecting anything.

prompt: Review a document-conversion pipeline where convert() wraps every failure — malformed input documents, HTTP 429 rate-limits from the OCR dependency, and disk-full errors — into a single ConversionError('conversion failed') with the original cause discarded; the batch runner catches ConversionError and re-queues every failed job, so malformed documents retry forever alongside genuinely transient rate-limit failures.
location_hint: the catch-all rethrow inside convert() and the re-queue-on-ConversionError policy in the batch runner
rationale: One failure shape erases the domain/transport/infrastructure distinction and retryability — terminal malformed input is indistinguishable from a retryable 429, producing infinite retries — SD-S-5's core signal; the collapse happens mid-pipeline with the cause discarded, so neither guard branch (documented edge translation, top-level reporter) applies.

prompt: Review a ticketing service's hold-release job that frees expired seat holds section by section in a loop, where each section's database write sits in its own try/catch that logs at debug level and continues, and the job then reports success and marks the release batch complete; during a recent failover several section writes were rejected, leaving those seats stuck on hold for days while the batch showed green.
location_hint: the per-section try/catch-continue loop in the hold-release job and its unconditional success report
rationale: Failures on a state-changing path (releasing seat holds) are swallowed mid-path and the batch reports success despite partial application — SD-S-5's block-severity form, 'swallowed failures on state-changing paths'; a mid-loop debug-log-and-continue is not a top-level reporter, so the guard fails.

prompt: Review a calendar-sync client whose every remote operation returns bare `false` on any failure: request timeouts, 401 responses after a user revokes access, and provider-side validation rejects all collapse into the same boolean, and the sync scheduler interprets any `false` as 'retry on the next tick'. Accounts with revoked tokens have been hammering the provider on every tick for weeks, and validation errors never reach the user.
location_hint: the boolean-only failure returns in the calendar-sync client and the retry-on-false loop in the scheduler
rationale: A single failure shape (bare false) hides whether a failure is retryable (timeout) or terminal (revoked auth, validation reject), so the scheduler cannot make a correct retry decision — the 'or retryability' clause of SD-S-5's signal; the smallest action is named retryable-versus-terminal failure classes.

prompt: Review an HTTP API layer whose single error middleware catches every internally raised error and translates it at the edge per a mapping table documented in the repo: ValidationRejected becomes 422 problem+json (terminal), DependencyTimeout becomes 503 with Retry-After (retryable), and anything else becomes 500 with an incident id; code below the middleware raises and propagates these typed errors untouched, and the full cause chain is logged at the edge.
location_hint: the error-translation middleware at the HTTP edge
rationale: A single middleware catching everything resembles error-contract collapse, but the guard — 'documented edge translation with mapped failure classes' — is met precisely: typed failures propagate internally, and the one catch site is a documented edge translation that preserves class and retryability (422 terminal vs 503 with Retry-After).

prompt: Review a backup CLI whose main() holds the program's only catch-all: it maps UsageError to exit code 2 with a usage hint, RemoteUnavailable to exit code 3 with a 'safe to re-run' note, and anything else to exit code 1 with a stack trace on stderr; every function below main() lets these typed errors propagate, and the state-changing upload step aborts the run on first failure rather than continuing.
location_hint: the catch-all block in the backup CLI's main()
rationale: A catch-everything block looks like swallowing, but SD-S-5's guard names this exact shape — 'a top-level reporter at the entrypoint': mid-path failures stay typed and distinct, state-changing failures abort the run, and the single entrypoint handler only reports and encodes the failure class into exit codes.

prompt: Review a payments repo whose settlement module embeds the marketplace fee-calculation rules: the pricing team owns and changes those rules but must land every change as a PR into the payments repo under payments-team CODEOWNERS review, and the past year of git history shows the fee-rule files changed almost exclusively by pricing engineers, with three changes delayed for weeks and one reverted after a payments reviewer misjudged a pricing rule.
location_hint: the fee-calculation rules inside the payments repo's settlement module (payments CODEOWNERS gate, pricing-team commit history)
rationale: The module boundary crosses the real decision owner — code the pricing team owns lives inside a payments-owned boundary behind a gatekeeper without the domain knowledge, with human and history evidence (delays, a bad revert) — SD-T-1's 'boundary crosses owner'; two distinct teams in a large org rule out both guard branches.

prompt: Review a monorepo orders-service where returns handling is maintained day-to-day by the returns team while the rest belongs to the orders team, yet both features are implemented through the same shared modules with no written contract and no CODEOWNERS split; the last two quarters of history show repeated cross-team merge conflicts in those files and two incidents where an orders refactor silently broke returns flows.
location_hint: the shared modules inside orders-service edited by both the orders and returns teams
rationale: One boundary contains two de-facto owners with no stated contract, and the crossing shows up in history as conflicts and cross-team breakage — SD-T-1 at warn severity since the owners are known; the smallest action is to align the boundary with an owner or state an explicit contract.

prompt: Review a data-platform repo where the ingest and enrichment stages are deeply interleaved — they share internal staging tables and a deploy unit — which a newly arrived architect flagged as 'two teams tangled together'; the org chart and CODEOWNERS show both stages are built and operated by the single data-platform team, which deliberately co-locates them and reviews every change as one owner.
location_hint: the ingest and enrichment stages of the data-platform repo
rationale: The interleaving suggests a boundary crossing owners, but SD-T-1's guard — 'shared owner' — applies: one team owns both stages end to end and reviews them as a unit, so no boundary crosses an owner; whatever coupling exists is not an ownership mismatch.

prompt: Review a three-person startup's single repo for a booking product: one backend developer wrote and maintains the api/, billing/, and scheduling/ folders, module boundaries were drawn by feature rather than by team, and there is no CODEOWNERS file, no team split, and no plan to hire into separate teams this year.
location_hint: the module layout of the three-person startup's repo
rationale: Boundaries that match no organizational owner look like an ownership mismatch, but the guard — 'small project' — applies: with effectively one owner for everything and no team structure to mismatch against, boundary-versus-owner alignment carries no signal here and nothing should be flagged.

prompt: Review an order-management service where every module uses the single glossary term Shipment for the delivery concept; the courier API's JSON is converted at a gateway adapter into an owned Shipment value object with validated invariants before anything else sees it; failures form a small sealed set — OrderRejected (terminal) and CourierUnavailable (retryable, carrying a retry-after) — propagated typed internally and mapped once at the HTTP edge per a documented table; and the fulfillment team owns the whole service with matching CODEOWNERS.
location_hint: whole service
rationale: Deliberately well-formed on every axis this group checks: one name per concept (no SD-S-1), one model per concept with no drifting copies (no SD-S-2), the external courier shape translated at the edge (no SD-S-4), a typed failure taxonomy with retryability and a documented edge mapping (no SD-S-5), and the boundary aligned with a single owning team (no SD-T-1).

prompt: Review a subscription-billing service where RenewalTerm is the one canonical model for renewal periods, owned by the billing module and used by callers only through its public API; the external tax-rate provider's response is mapped inside the provider adapter into an internal TaxRate value object; every failure is raised as either PlanConfigInvalid (terminal) or TaxProviderTimeout (retryable), with the single retry policy attached only to the retryable class in the outbound adapter; and the service catalog records the billing team as owner of the module.
location_hint: whole service
rationale: Well-designed across the group's concerns: canonical vocabulary and a single owned model with API-only access (no SD-S-1/S-2), the external tax shape translated at the adapter edge (no SD-S-4), a named terminal-versus-retryable taxonomy handled at one owning layer (no SD-S-5), and documented, aligned ownership (no SD-T-1).

prompt: In a billing service, `billing/invoice.py` imports `billing/customer.py` at module top to apply per-customer discount tiers when totaling an invoice, while `billing/customer.py` imports `billing/invoice.py` to compute a customer's lifetime spend from stored invoice totals. The team broke the resulting ImportError by moving one import inside a function body, and both modules now call each other's functions on every request.
location_hint: billing/invoice.py <-> billing/customer.py mutual imports (one deferred into a function body)
rationale: The module-level dependency points both ways — a real compile-time/import cycle visible on both graph and static evidence layers. The function-body import only hides the cycle from the interpreter rather than removing it, so the 'runtime callback without compile-time cycle' guard does not apply; splitting the shared totals contract or inverting one direction is the card's smallest action.

prompt: In a shift-scheduling server, `scheduler/planner.ts` statically imports `notifications/reminders.ts` and calls `queueReminder(shift)` after each assignment, while `notifications/reminders.ts` statically imports `scheduler/planner.ts` to call `getShiftWindow(shiftId)` when formatting reminder text. The app only boots because module evaluation order happens to initialize the planner first, and a recent barrel-export reorder produced `undefined is not a function` errors at startup.
location_hint: circular static imports between scheduler/planner.ts and notifications/reminders.ts
rationale: Both modules hold compile-time import edges to each other and correctness depends on evaluation-order luck — a live two-way dependency, not a runtime callback through an owned interface. Extracting the shift-window contract into its own module or inverting the reminder call breaks the cycle, matching the card's smallest action.

prompt: A log-parsing crate's `parser/engine.rs` defines a `ProgressSink` trait with `fn on_chunk(&self, done: u64, total: u64)` and accepts `&dyn ProgressSink` in `parse_stream`; the CLI module `cli/report.rs` implements `ProgressSink` to draw a progress bar and passes itself in when invoking the parser. At runtime the engine calls back into CLI code through the trait, but the dependency graph has a single static edge: `cli` depends on `parser`, and `parser` depends only on its own trait definition.
location_hint: parser-owned ProgressSink trait; one-way cli -> parser static edge
rationale: This is SD-C-1's false_positive_guard verbatim: a runtime callback without a compile-time cycle. The engine reaches outward only through an interface it owns, and all static edges point one way — this is the inverted structure the card's fix recommends, not the smell.

prompt: An inventory service's `inventory/replenishment.py` — the module deciding when and how much stock to reorder — imports the cloud vendor's queue SDK at the top, constructs the vendor client inline, and publishes reorder messages itself; its `plan_reorders()` function takes the vendor SDK's message-batch type as a parameter and reads vendor message attributes to decide whether a reorder was already requested.
location_hint: inventory/replenishment.py vendor-SDK import; vendor batch type in the plan_reorders() signature
rationale: Reorder policy statically depends on vendor/storage detail — vendor imports, client construction, and vendor types inside core decision signatures — with no policy-owned port in sight. The dependency arrow points from policy inward to adapter concerns, exactly the inversion SD-C-2 blocks for new code.

prompt: In a Java pricing module, the domain class `pricing/DiscountPolicy` imports the web framework's `RequestContext` and reads the current HTTP request's locale header inside `roundFor()` to pick rounding rules, and the pricing entities carry the ORM's column and table annotations so persistence mapping compiles into the domain jar. Unit-testing a discount calculation now requires booting the framework's request scope and having the ORM on the classpath.
location_hint: pricing/DiscountPolicy import of the framework RequestContext; ORM annotations on pricing entities
rationale: Pricing policy holds static edges to HTTP-framework and ORM detail — 'policy imports framework, storage, or vendor detail' verbatim. Locale should arrive as a plain parameter and mapping should live in an outward adapter; no policy-owned port or plugin contract exists, so the guard cannot clear it.

prompt: A payments domain package `payments/core` defines its own `ReceiptStore` interface with `save(Receipt)` and `findByOrder(OrderId)`, and `SettlementPolicy` calls only that interface; the database-backed implementation lives outward in `payments/adapters/sqlstore`, which imports `payments/core` and is wired in at the composition root. A reviewer scanning stack traces sees settlement code invoking storage operations and suspects the policy layer depends on the database.
location_hint: ReceiptStore port defined inside payments/core; adapter imports point adapter -> policy only
rationale: The storage-flavored call site is a policy-owned port contract — SD-C-2's false_positive_guard exactly. All static edges run from adapter to policy, and no framework, storage, or vendor import exists inside `payments/core`, so the inversion the smell describes is absent.

prompt: In a monorepo, the `common/utils` package imported by all nine services has accumulated `calculateLateFee()`, `isVipCustomer()`, and `formatDunningNotice()` next to generic string and date helpers; commit history shows the billing team changed these three functions eleven times this quarter, each change rebuilding unrelated services, and a fulfillment service recently started calling `isVipCustomer()` directly for its own throttling.
location_hint: common/utils: calculateLateFee / isVipCustomer / formatDunningNotice
rationale: Volatile billing policy has migrated into the widely-imported shared core — static placement plus churn history, the card's two evidence layers — coupling unrelated services to billing rule changes and inviting cross-context policy reuse. These are not stable utilities, so the guard does not apply; the smallest action is moving the policy home to billing.

prompt: A `platform/shared` library consumed by both the clinic-scheduling service and the payroll service contains `MAX_CONSECUTIVE_SHIFTS` and `overtimeMultiplier(hours, contractType)`; the payroll team edits the multiplier table most sprints, each edit forces a scheduling redeploy, and last month a payroll-driven change to the constant silently tightened scheduling's shift validation for clinics.
location_hint: platform/shared overtime and consecutive-shift policy consumed by both scheduling and payroll
rationale: The shared core owns volatile policy spanning two bounded contexts, so churn in one context redeploys and behaviorally alters the other — the cross-context-owner variant SD-C-3 escalates to block. History (sprint-level churn) plus the cross-context behavioral bleed makes this a true positive with no stable-utility defense.

prompt: A `common/text` package used by every service exports `slugify()`, `truncateOnGrapheme()`, and `formatIsoDate()` as pure functions with pinned unit tests; version history shows no behavioral change in eighteen months apart from one dependency bump, and no service-specific rule has ever lived there. A reviewer flags the package because everything imports it, calling it a coupling magnet.
location_hint: common/text pure helpers with 18 months of unchanged history
rationale: SD-C-3's false_positive_guard is 'stable utility', and that is what this is: generic, policy-free helpers whose history shows no churn. High fan-in on a demonstrably stable utility is not gravity — nothing volatile has been absorbed, so there is no policy to move home.

prompt: A shipping-quote API keeps a module-level dict `_rate_cache` in `rates.py`; request handlers read and write it directly while computing quotes, and a nightly recalculation job clears and repopulates the same dict in place while requests are in flight. Support tickets show intermittently wrong quotes around 02:00 that no unit test reproduces, and two handlers disagree about whether entries hold pre- or post-surcharge values.
location_hint: rates.py module-level _rate_cache shared by request handlers and the nightly job
rationale: A hidden module-global mutable cache couples independent request flows and a background job with no owner or lifetime scope — cross-request state, which the card blocks. Static evidence (the global dict, direct handler mutation) plus runtime evidence (time-correlated wrong quotes) match SD-C-4's two evidence layers; neither guard arm (immutable config, scoped lifetime) applies.

prompt: A document-conversion library exposes `ConverterRegistry.instance()`, a process-wide singleton whose `setDefaultDpi()` and `registerFont()` mutate shared maps; the batch-export pipeline tunes it to 300 DPI with print fonts while the web preview endpoint sets 96 DPI with screen fonts, so whichever flow configured it last determines every flow's output, and the test suite passes only in one execution order.
location_hint: ConverterRegistry.instance() global mutable registry reconfigured by both the pipeline and the preview flow
rationale: A mutable singleton couples two otherwise independent flows through last-writer-wins global state — order-dependent output and order-dependent tests are the classic runtime signature of 'globals, singletons, or caches couple flows'. Each flow should own a converter configuration passed through its own scope, the card's smallest action.

prompt: A file-sync daemon loads `settings.toml` once at startup into a frozen dataclass bound to module-level `CONFIG`; every handler reads `CONFIG.chunk_size` and `CONFIG.endpoint`, nothing assigns to it after load, and reload requires a process restart by design. A reviewer flags the module-level global as shared state coupling the sync flows.
location_hint: module-level frozen CONFIG loaded once at startup
rationale: SD-C-4's guard names 'immutable config' as the cleared case, and this is it verbatim: the global is frozen after startup and never mutated, so no flow can affect another through it. A read-only constant is not hidden mutable state, however global its binding.

prompt: A catalog API's middleware creates a `RequestCache` per incoming request, stores it on the request context, and disposes it when the response is written; handlers memoize product-category lookups in it so one request never recomputes the same lookup twice. A reviewer sees cache writes inside handlers and flags hidden mutable state coupling requests.
location_hint: per-request RequestCache created and disposed by middleware
rationale: SD-C-4's guard also clears an 'explicit scoped lifetime', which this cache has: an owning middleware creates it per request and disposes it at response end, so no state crosses requests and no flows are coupled. Mutation inside a well-scoped lifetime is the healthy pattern, not the smell.

prompt: Three services each carry their own copy of the address-normalization routine: `checkout` forked it to add apartment-unit handling, `logistics` forked it again for rural-route formats, and the original in `crm` still lowercases street names differently; no owner or plan exists to reconverge them, and a postcode-validation bug fixed in the `logistics` copy last month still corrupts labels generated through the other two.
location_hint: address-normalization forks in checkout, logistics, and crm
rationale: One shared concern exists as three concurrently diverging forks with no named convergence owner, and fixes no longer propagate — the first signal clause of SD-C-5 and the unbounded divergence its severity line blocks. The smallest action is naming a convergence owner and plan, not merely deduplicating text.

prompt: An internal telemetry pipeline's collector now emits event-schema v5 while its two downstream consumers still parse v3 and silently ignore unknown fields; no rule bounds how far consumers may lag and nobody owns deciding when they must catch up, and a v5 fraud-scoring field was dropped by both consumers for an entire quarter before anyone noticed.
location_hint: telemetry event schema: producer at v5, consumers at v3, no skew bound or convergence owner
rationale: This is SD-C-5's second signal clause verbatim: unbounded internal producer/consumer skew with no convergence owner. The quarter of silent data loss is the consequence of nothing forcing convergence; bounding the skew and naming an owner is the card's smallest action.

prompt: During a two-release migration, a ledger service accepts both v2 and v3 posting messages; the migration record names the payments-platform team as convergence owner, caps allowed skew at one version, tracks remaining v2 producers on a dashboard, and schedules deletion of the v2 path for the release after the last producer flips. A reviewer sees two live parser versions for one message type and wants to flag divergence.
location_hint: ledger posting-message v2/v3 dual-accept during an owned, exit-dated migration
rationale: SD-C-5's guard clears 'bounded skew with a named convergence owner and exit', and all three elements are explicit here: a one-version skew cap, a named owning team, and a scheduled deletion trigger. Two concurrent versions inside an owned, bounded, exit-dated migration are the managed case the guard protects.

prompt: A rate-limiting module ships exactly one implementation, a class named `TokenBucketLimiterV2`; the V1 implementation was deleted two quarters ago, every caller imports the single class, and the V2 survives only in the class name and a changelog entry. A reviewer greps for version suffixes and flags concurrent limiter implementations.
location_hint: single TokenBucketLimiterV2 implementation; V1 deleted, suffix is naming residue
rationale: SD-C-5's guard clears a 'single supported version': exactly one implementation exists and every consumer uses it. A version-suffixed name is residue of a completed convergence, not a concurrent fork — there is no divergence to own and no skew to bound.

prompt: A CRM's contact-import endpoint spawns a detached async task per CSV row to enrich and persist the record, discarding every task handle; nothing joins or tracks the tasks, row-level failures surface nowhere, a service shutdown mid-import silently truncates the batch, and there is no way to cancel a stuck import.
location_hint: contact-import handler: per-row detached tasks with discarded handles
rationale: Spawned work has no lifetime, join, or cancellation owner — the first signal clause of SD-C-6 — and it is state-changing work whose failures are unobservable and whose shutdown behavior truncates data, the detached-work case the card blocks. An owning scope that joins or cancels the batch is the smallest action.

prompt: A report service's HTTP handler receives the request's cancellation token, but `RenderPipeline.run()` internally starts three page-rasterizing workers on a fresh, never-cancelled context; when a client disconnects, the handler returns immediately while the workers keep rasterizing for minutes, pinning CPU and holding the output-file lock until they finish on their own.
location_hint: RenderPipeline.run(): workers started on a fresh context, caller cancellation not propagated
rationale: Caller cancellation exists but does not propagate across the pipeline boundary — SD-C-6's second signal clause — so abandoned work outlives its request with no owner able to stop it, with observable runtime cost (pinned CPU, held lock). Threading the caller's token through the worker scope is the card's propagation fix.

prompt: A mapping service fans out batch geocoding across a structured concurrency scope: the request handler opens a task group that inherits the request's cancellation token, spawns one lookup task per address, cancels remaining siblings on the first hard failure, and joins all children before returning the assembled result. A reviewer sees dozens of spawned tasks per request and flags background work.
location_hint: request-handler task group owning geocoding fan-out; join before return, token inherited
rationale: SD-C-6's guard clears 'supervised or scoped work with a named owner', and the task group is exactly that owner: it bounds every child's lifetime, joins before returning, and propagates the caller's cancellation. Spawning many tasks is not the smell — detachment is, and nothing here is detached.

prompt: A subscription-billing service keeps proration and dunning policy in `billing/core`, which defines the `PaymentGateway` and `InvoiceStore` ports it owns; adapters in `billing/adapters` implement those ports and are wired at the composition root, per-request state lives in a DI scope disposed with each request, and the retry-billing job runs under the platform scheduler, which restarts it on failure and stops it at shutdown through a propagated cancellation signal. All consumers read the single current invoice-message schema, and the only shared code is a currency-math library unchanged in a year.
location_hint: billing/core ports, billing/adapters wiring at the composition root, scheduler-owned retry job
rationale: Every concern this family probes appears in its guarded, healthy form: one-way dependencies through policy-owned ports (no cycle, no policy-to-adapter edge), a stable shared utility rather than absorbed policy, request-scoped rather than hidden state, one supported schema version, and supervised background work with propagated cancellation. Review should surface nothing from SD-C-1 through SD-C-6.

prompt: A log-parsing CLI reads its flags into an immutable options struct, streams records through a pure `parse/` core that depends only on the standard library, and fans work across a worker pool created in `main` with a context cancelled on SIGINT, waiting on all workers before printing the summary. Output formatting lives in `format/`, which imports `parse/` types one-way, and the tool documents a single supported input format.
location_hint: main-owned joined worker pool; one-way format/ -> parse/ dependency; immutable options struct
rationale: The design shows the healthy counterpart of each family concern it touches: acyclic one-way module dependencies, a dependency-free pure core instead of policy importing adapters, no shared mutable globals (immutable options), main-owned concurrency that is joined and cancellable, and a single supported format. There is no cycle, inversion, gravity, hidden state, divergence, or unowned work to report.

prompt: A payroll service's tax module defines an ITaxRateSource interface, an abstract TaxRateSourceBase with template hooks, and a TaxRateSourceFactory that switches on a one-member enum; the sole implementation is StaticTableTaxRateSource, and repository history shows no second source has appeared in the 18 months since the scaffolding landed. All callers obtain the source through the factory.
location_hint: ITaxRateSource / TaxRateSourceBase / TaxRateSourceFactory scaffolding around the single StaticTableTaxRateSource
rationale: Interface plus abstract base plus factory keyed on a one-member enum, serving exactly one implementation with 18 months of history and no second variant, is imagined variation: no real boundary is being protected and no variation is proven. Smallest action is to inline the concrete source and delete the scaffolding.

prompt: A media pipeline exposes a generic TranscodeStep<TIn, TOut, TCtx> strategy contract plus a StepRegistry and a fluent PipelineBuilder with beforeRun/afterRun/onError extension hooks; exactly one concrete step (Mp4ToHlsStep) is registered anywhere, every hook is an empty no-op default, and the builder is always invoked with the same hardcoded chain of one.
location_hint: TranscodeStep strategy contract, StepRegistry, and PipelineBuilder hook surface
rationale: A three-type-parameter strategy, a registry, and a hook surface all serving a single concrete step with no-op hooks is machinery built for variation nobody has; the static shape shows one registrant and one fixed chain, so the variation is imagined, not proven.

prompt: An invoicing domain defines a PaymentGatewayPort interface owned by the billing policy package; its only production implementation is AcmePayHttpAdapter, which wraps the external card processor's SDK, and unit tests substitute an in-memory fake through the same port. A reviewer notes the interface has just one real implementation and suggests deleting it as over-abstraction.
location_hint: PaymentGatewayPort with the single AcmePayHttpAdapter implementation
rationale: One production implementation is the surface signal of speculative abstraction, but the port sits on a real boundary — it keeps the external processor's SDK out of billing policy and is exercised by a test fake — which is exactly the 'real boundary' branch of the SD-W-1 guard, so it must not be flagged.

prompt: A notification module declares a ChannelSender interface with three shipped implementations — EmailSender, SmsSender, and WebhookSender — chosen per recipient at runtime from stored preferences; a new teammate flags the interface as over-engineering because the vast majority of traffic goes through email.
location_hint: ChannelSender interface and its three runtime-selected implementations
rationale: The variation is proven, not imagined: three live implementations are selected at runtime by stored data, so the abstraction carries real polymorphism regardless of traffic skew — the 'proven variation' branch of the guard clears it.

prompt: In a warehouse system, every controller call goes through InventoryService, whose twelve public methods each contain exactly one line delegating to the identically named method on InventoryRepository with the same parameters and return type; the service adds no validation, mapping, caching, transactions, retries, or logging, and nothing else references it.
location_hint: InventoryService's twelve one-line delegations to InventoryRepository
rationale: Twelve method-for-method one-line forwards with identical signatures and zero added behavior is meaningless forwarding; the layer is not a compatibility, logging, retry, transaction, or translation owner, so it should be removed or given real ownership.

prompt: A clinic-scheduling codebase routes all appointment reads through ScheduleManager, which relays each call unchanged to ScheduleQueryHelper, which relays it unchanged to the ORM query object; neither intermediate class transforms arguments, results, or errors, and neither owns retries, transactions, logging, or any compatibility surface.
location_hint: ScheduleManager -> ScheduleQueryHelper double forwarding chain over the ORM query object
rationale: Two stacked layers that only relay calls add navigation and change cost with zero ownership; with none of the guard's legitimate roles (compatibility, logging, retry, transaction, translation) present, the forwarding is meaningless and the layers should collapse.

prompt: An order-sync component wraps the raw ERP client in ErpGateway, whose method names mirror the client one-to-one and whose bodies look like thin forwards, but each call executes inside the gateway's retry policy with exponential backoff and idempotency keys, and write methods open and commit the unit-of-work transaction. A reviewer flags the gateway as a needless wrapper because of the mirrored method names.
location_hint: ErpGateway wrapping the raw ERP client
rationale: Mirrored names make it look like meaningless forwarding, but the layer is the retry and transaction owner — two of the SD-W-2 guard's named ownership roles — so it earns its place; and backoff/idempotency is technical resilience, not domain policy, so it is not an adapter deciding domain policy either.

prompt: A reporting library's LegacyReportFacade re-exposes the frozen v1 API, and each method body is a single delegation to the new ReportEngine equivalent, mapping renamed parameters and defaulting removed options; it is documented as the compatibility surface that keeps pre-2.0 integrators compiling, with removal scheduled for the next major release.
location_hint: LegacyReportFacade delegating to ReportEngine
rationale: One-line delegations look like a pass-through layer, but the facade is a declared compatibility and translation owner (frozen v1 surface, parameter mapping, scheduled removal) — exactly the 'compatibility ... or translation owner' guard — so the forwarding is meaningful and must not be flagged.

prompt: ReplenishmentPlanner computes restock quantities for a grocery chain, but over time it has also absorbed the supplier-selection tiebreak rule, the customer-facing backorder message wording choice, and the finance holdback percentage; git log shows procurement and finance changes repeatedly landing in the planner file while its forecasting logic rarely changes.
location_hint: ReplenishmentPlanner's supplier-selection, backorder-messaging, and finance-holdback decisions
rationale: Restock forecasting, supplier selection, customer messaging, and finance holdback are unrelated decisions sharing one owner, and the history evidence (procurement/finance edits landing in the planner) is the classic drift signature; each decision has a natural owner elsewhere and one should move there.

prompt: In a freight-billing codebase, TariffCalculator computes lane tariffs, but it also decides which shipments get routed to manual review and owns the file-naming convention for the finance export; three different teams file PRs against the calculator for reasons unrelated to tariff math, and none of the three concerns share data or rules.
location_hint: TariffCalculator's manual-review routing and export-naming decisions
rationale: Tariff math, review routing, and export conventions are unrelated decisions co-owned by one class, evidenced by three teams editing it for disjoint reasons — responsibility drift, not cohesion; the smallest action is moving one decision (e.g. review routing) to its natural owner.

prompt: During checkout, CheckoutCoordinator calls the cart validator, then the payment authorizer, then the fulfillment scheduler in order, holding no business rules of its own — each step's decision logic lives in its own module and the coordinator only sequences them for this one flow. A reviewer worries the coordinator 'touches too many concerns'.
location_hint: CheckoutCoordinator's step sequencing
rationale: The coordinator references many concerns but owns none of their decisions — the co-location is sequencing only, which is the SD-B-1 guard ('temporary sequencing only'); every decision remains with its natural owner, so no responsibility has drifted.

prompt: An event-ticketing system stores seats_remaining on the performance row; the box-office sales path, the refund processor, and a nightly partner-reseller sync each update the column directly with their own SQL, each separately re-implementing the no-oversell check — and the sync's version omits it entirely.
location_hint: seats_remaining column written directly by sales, refunds, and the reseller sync
rationale: Three independent writers mutate the same state and each carries its own copy of the oversell invariant, one of which has already diverged — the invariant has no single owner and is leaking; the fix is to name one owner and route all mutation through it.

prompt: A campsite-booking platform keeps a reservation status field ('held', 'confirmed', 'expired', 'cancelled'); the REST handler flips it on user actions, a background expiry job flips it when holds time out, and a support-console script flips it during refunds — each with its own inline transition rules, and the expiry job has been observed overwriting a concurrent 'confirmed' back to 'expired'.
location_hint: reservation status transitions spread across the REST handler, expiry job, and support script
rationale: The status state machine has three mutation owners with divergent inline transition rules and a demonstrated lost update (confirmed overwritten to expired); state-owner blur is the root cause, and mutation needs to route through one named owner of the transition invariant.

prompt: In a ledger service, balance changes are requested by the payments API, the fee engine, and the dispute workflow, but all three call LedgerAccount.post(entry) on the aggregate, which is the only code that touches the balance and enforces double-entry and non-overdraft rules inside one transaction. A reviewer counts 'three writers of balance' and raises an alarm.
location_hint: LedgerAccount aggregate posting entries on behalf of three calling workflows
rationale: Many callers request mutation, but a single explicit aggregate owns the state and enforces its invariants transactionally — precisely the SD-B-2 guard ('explicit aggregate or transaction owner'); counting callers is not counting mutation owners, so nothing should be flagged.

prompt: A config-parsing package builds an internal nested dictionary keyed by section paths like 'net.retry.max', with private sentinel objects for unset values; four downstream modules import the parser's module-level _tree and walk it directly, and one also checks isinstance(node, _Unset) against the parser's private sentinel class.
location_hint: downstream imports of the parser's _tree structure and _Unset sentinel class
rationale: Callers depend on the private tree layout and sentinel class rather than an owned API — underscore-private access from outside the package is neither an owned extension nor a stable DTO — so any internal reshape breaks four modules; the parser owes them an exposed, owned API.

prompt: A document-archive service returns its ORM entity objects straight through its public API; three consuming packages navigate lazy-loaded relations like folder.documents[0].revisions and rely on column-named attributes, and when the service team renames a column and splits the revisions table, all three consumers break.
location_hint: archive service API returning ORM entities that consumers navigate directly
rationale: The persistence-internal shape (entity graph, lazy relations, column-named attributes) has become the de facto contract, so callers depend on internal shape instead of a stable DTO and persistence refactors ripple to every consumer — the core internals-leakage signal, fixed by exposing an owned API.

prompt: An insurance quoting engine exposes QuoteResult, a versioned and documented plain record (line items, totals, currency) that happens to mirror several of the engine's internal fields; consumers destructure it freely. A reviewer objects that consumers are 'coupled to the engine's data shape' and wants the record hidden.
location_hint: QuoteResult record consumed by callers
rationale: Consumers depend on a deliberately exported, versioned, documented DTO — an owned stable contract, which is exactly the SD-B-3 guard ('stable DTO'); the fact that the published record mirrors internal fields does not make consuming it a leak.

prompt: A build tool lets plugins subclass its published Reporter base class and override onTaskFinished(event); a plugin's subclass accesses the protected self.output_stream member that the base class documents for exactly this extension purpose. A static scanner flags the plugin for 'reaching into the tool's internals'.
location_hint: plugin subclass using Reporter's documented protected member
rationale: The access point is an owned extension surface — a documented protected member on a published extension base class — which the SD-B-3 guard ('owned extension') explicitly clears; this is designed extension, not dependence on internal shape.

prompt: A card-processor webhook adapter parses gateway callback payloads, but it also decides whether a failed charge enters the dunning retry sequence, waives late fees for customers it looks up in a VIP table, and cancels the subscription after a third failure; the billing domain module contains none of these rules.
location_hint: webhook adapter's dunning, fee-waiver, and cancellation decisions
rationale: Dunning entry, fee waivers, and cancellation thresholds are domain policy, yet they live only inside the transport adapter and the domain has no home for them — the adapter decides domain policy instead of translating callbacks, so the policy must move home.

prompt: In a car-rental system, the persistence adapter VehicleRowMapper applies business rules while converting database rows to domain objects: it downgrades a vehicle's rental class when mileage crosses a threshold and marks vehicles 'retired' after five model years, so the domain layer never sees the raw values and does not own those cut-offs.
location_hint: VehicleRowMapper's class-downgrade and retirement rules
rationale: Mileage-based downgrade and age-based retirement are domain classification decisions embedded in a row-mapping adapter; because mapping silently applies them, the domain neither sees the raw data nor owns the thresholds — adapter-owned policy, not representation translation.

prompt: A weather-data adapter converts a vendor feed into internal readings: it renames fields, converts Fahrenheit to Celsius, coerces the vendor's -999 missing-value marker to null, and normalizes timestamps to UTC. A reviewer flags the unit conversion and sentinel handling as 'business logic hidden in the adapter'.
location_hint: weather feed adapter's unit, sentinel, and timezone normalization
